title: Mexico’s server exports conceal a tariff drag shared with Canada
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Canada’s goods exports to the United States fell about 10% while Mexico’s rose about 16%, comparing the twelve months to April 2026 with calendar 2024. Chris Avalos, Musa Orak and Avani Pradhan find that sectors facing higher US tariffs subsequently performed worse in both countries. A surge in Mexican computer and server exports outweighed losses elsewhere. The headline divergence consequently gives a misleading picture of how exposed industries fared, and the nominal value of the shipments gives an incomplete picture of how much income Mexico retained.

The exposure measure applies announced rates and exemptions to each country’s 2024 US import basket. It incorporates eligibility under the US–Mexico–Canada Agreement and variation in product-specific tariffs. Using fixed weights prevents a later switch into low-tariff products from mechanically reducing the exposure measure. It does not make policy assignment random: sectors were deliberately targeted and estimated compliance can itself reflect firms’ reactions. The weighted effective rate is 5.4% for Canada and 8.0% for Mexico. More than half the sectors in each country face rates below 1%, while tariffs on metals leave a small set of sectors far more exposed (Figure 1 and footnotes 3–4).

The monthly comparison within each country holds persistent sector differences and economy-wide monthly shocks constant. An additional 10 percentage points of tariff exposure is associated with approximately 7.4% weaker US-bound exports after March 2025 in the pooled baseline. Separate estimates are 4.9% weaker for Canada and 11.8% weaker for Mexico. The test for a difference between the country estimates has a p-value of 0.23. The point estimates alone cannot establish a larger underlying response in Mexico. The comparison also removes shocks affecting all exporters in a country, so the estimated effect cannot be applied to total exports or GDP (Table 1).

Several checks sharpen the interpretation. Omitting metals eliminates the negative Canadian point estimate, whereas the Mexican estimate remains negative. Controlling for US imports from third countries shrinks Mexico’s estimate considerably. Comparing exports to US and other destinations within sectors produces an estimated 11.2% relative shortfall for exposed Mexican sectors per 10 points of exposure. Canada's estimate is negative but imprecise. The monthly comparisons detect no differential pre-trend, and Mexico’s baseline differential reaches about −18% in spring 2026. Other US-specific sector shocks could still contribute. Exports to other markets may also respond to US tariffs, complicating the choice of comparison group (Figure 2, appendix Figure A1 and footnote 5).

The export decomposition in Figure 3 reconciles these patterns. Machinery contributes 17.3 percentage points to Mexico’s 15.6% total growth. US imports of computers and related units from Mexico climbed from $48 billion in 2024 to $106 billion in the year to April 2026, accounting for 96% of the increase in machinery imports from Mexico. The authors link this rise to US data-centre investment. Mexican plants assemble servers using substantial imported components, so gross export revenue overstates the domestic value added. Excluding machinery, Mexican exports fell around 2%; the median Mexican sector saw a 5.2% fall. The decomposition measures concentration, with no forecast of how long the order growth will last.

In Canada, mineral fuels and vehicles together account for about five percentage points of the 10.5% fall, and the median sector’s exports declined 6.4%. Weakness extended beyond the metals sectors that account for much of the estimated tariff relationship. For a portfolio assessment, the distinction matters on both sides of the border. An exporter’s US customer base, product duties and imported-input content can give a substantially different exposure to AI or tariffs from that suggested by its country’s aggregate export figures. The authors quantify trade values and sector differences without translating these into margin forecasts or currency targets.

questions.question: How much of the server boom becomes income for Mexican producers and workers?
questions.detail: The paper traces most of the machinery increase to computer shipments and identifies substantial imported components. It does not quantify the domestic margin on each additional unit. For an exposure linked to Mexican growth, compare the equipment categories in Mexican import and export records, manufacturing value-added data, wages and assemblers’ accounts. The Banco de México quarterly report cited by the authors gives a starting point.

questions.question: How much of Mexico’s sectoral differential reflects US demand for particular products?
questions.detail: The destination comparison favours a US-specific effect, while controlling for third-country imports materially reduces the baseline Mexican estimate. Those outcomes imply different sensitivities to changes in tariff policy. Use product-level US customs values and quantities, matched demand indicators and the cited sectoral exposure measure. Check whether the differential survives within similar products and before and after their precise tariff dates.

questions.question: Can Canadian exporters replace lost US sales without giving up margins?
questions.detail: The study finds broad weakness and an imprecise comparison between US and other destinations. It does not establish that reorientation preserved revenue, volumes or profits. Examine destination-level quantities and unit values alongside freight and compliance costs. The Bank of Canada business evidence cited in the article and exporters’ own disclosures could distinguish active market development from a shift in destination shares caused by falling US orders.
